pages.question: A 46-year-old man with newly diagnosed metabolic syndrome presents for a follow-up appointment. He meets four of five criteria: waist circumference 108 cm, fasting glucose 114 mg/dL, triglycerides 210 mg/dL, and blood pressure 138/88 mmHg. His HDL is 42 mg/dL. He takes no medications. His 10-year ASCVD risk is 8.4%. He asks whether he needs to start medications immediately or whether lifestyle changes can make a meaningful difference. He is motivated but overwhelmed and says he does not know where to start. He has 15 minutes remaining in the visit. Which of the following represents the most appropriate brief counseling intervention for this patient during this visit?

Counsel the patient that a 5–7% weight loss through a modest daily caloric deficit of 500–750 kcal combined with at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week has strong evidence for reducing all five metabolic syndrome components and reducing diabetes risk by up to 58%, and collaboratively identify one specific dietary change and one specific physical activity goal he can start this week

pages.question: A 46-year-old man with newly diagnosed metabolic syndrome presents for a follow-up appointment. He meets four of five criteria: waist circumference 108 cm, fasting glucose 114 mg/dL, triglycerides 210 mg/dL, and blood pressure 138/88 mmHg. His HDL is 42 mg/dL. He takes no medications. His 10-year ASCVD risk is 8.4%. He asks whether he needs to start medications immediately or whether lifestyle changes can make a meaningful difference. He is motivated but overwhelmed and says he does not know where to start. He has 15 minutes remaining in the visit. Which of the following represents the most appropriate brief counseling intervention for this patient during this visit?

answers.text:
Initiate metformin, a statin, and an ACE inhibitor simultaneously to address all components of metabolic syndrome pharmacologically, since lifestyle changes alone are insufficient for meaningful clinical improvement
(16.67%)

Counsel the patient that a 5–7% weight loss through a modest daily caloric deficit of 500–750 kcal combined with at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week has strong evidence for reducing all five metabolic syndrome components and reducing diabetes risk by up to 58%, and collaboratively identify one specific dietary change and one specific physical activity goal he can start this week
(83.33%)

Advise the patient to eliminate all carbohydrates and begin high-intensity interval training six days per week to achieve rapid reversal of metabolic syndrome within 30 days
(0%)

Reassure the patient that metabolic syndrome is a laboratory construct without clinical significance and that no intervention is needed until he develops frank type 2 diabetes or a cardiovascular event
(0%)

Refer the patient to a registered dietitian and schedule follow-up in one year to reassess metabolic syndrome criteria, as specialized nutrition counseling is more effective than brief physician intervention
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Brief lifestyle counseling for metabolic syndrome should prioritize two evidence-based targets: a 5–7% reduction in body weight through modest caloric deficit, and 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity physical activity. These two interventions have the strongest evidence for reducing visceral adiposity, improving all five metabolic syndrome components, and reducing progression to type 2 diabetes. Practical, specific, achievable goals are more effective than comprehensive dietary overhauls in brief clinical encounters.
(Choice A)
Initiate metformin, a statin, and an ACE inhibitor simultaneously to address all components of metabolic syndrome pharmacologically, since lifestyle changes alone are insufficient for meaningful clinical improvement
This approach is incorrect because lifestyle modification, not pharmacotherapy, is the evidence-based first-line treatment for metabolic syndrome. While individual components (hypertension, dyslipidemia) may eventually require medications if lifestyle intervention fails to achieve targets, simultaneous initiation of multiple medications without attempting lifestyle modification contradicts established guidelines from the American Heart Association and NCEP ATP III. The underlying pathophysiology of metabolic syndrome centers on visceral adiposity and insulin resistance, which are best addressed through weight reduction and physical activity. Medications treat symptoms but do not address the root cause.
(Choice B)
Counsel the patient that a 5–7% weight loss through a modest daily caloric deficit of 500–750 kcal combined with at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week has strong evidence for reducing all five metabolic syndrome components and reducing diabetes risk by up to 58%, and collaboratively identify one specific dietary change and one specific physical activity goal he can start this week
Lifestyle modification targeting visceral adiposity is the evidence-based first-line management for metabolic syndrome, with strong evidence demonstrating that even modest weight loss produces clinically meaningful improvements across all five metabolic syndrome components. The landmark Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) demonstrated that lifestyle intervention targeting 7% weight loss and 150 minutes per week of physical activity reduced progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes by 58% — superior to metformin (31% reduction). Mechanism: even modest weight loss of 5–7% preferentially reduces visceral adipose tissue (VAT reduces proportionally more than subcutaneous fat with energy deficit), decreasing portal FFA delivery to the liver, improving hepatic insulin sensitivity, reducing VLDL-triglyceride secretion, raising HDL, lowering blood pressure through reduced hyperinsulinemia and sympathetic tone, and improving fasting glucose. Physical activity independently reduces VAT through increased skeletal muscle fatty acid oxidation, AMPK activation improving insulin sensitivity, and increased energy expenditure. For a 15-minute brief counseling encounter, evidence-based communication strategies include: framing the 5–7% goal concretely (for this patient, approximately 15 lbs); explaining that weight loss this modest can meaningfully improve all his laboratory values; using collaborative goal-setting to identify one specific, achievable dietary change (e.g., eliminating sugar-sweetened beverages or reducing portion size at dinner) and one specific physical activity goal (e.g., 30-minute walk five days per week); and scheduling a follow-up in 4–6 weeks to reinforce progress. Medications are not first-line for metabolic syndrome itself — individual components such as hypertension or dyslipidemia may eventually require pharmacotherapy if lifestyle intervention is insufficient.
(Choice C)
Advise the patient to eliminate all carbohydrates and begin high-intensity interval training six days per week to achieve rapid reversal of metabolic syndrome within 30 days
Prescribing extreme dietary restriction (complete carbohydrate elimination) and aggressive exercise (HIIT six days per week) to a sedentary patient with metabolic syndrome is likely to produce rapid initial failure, injury risk, and disengagement. Evidence consistently shows that sustainable, gradual lifestyle changes produce better long-term outcomes than aggressive prescriptions that patients cannot maintain. The evidence-based target of 5–7% weight loss through a modest 500–750 kcal daily deficit and 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity activity is achievable, sustainable, and has the strongest long-term outcome data. Extreme prescriptions that overwhelm patients are counterproductive.
(Choice D)
Reassure the patient that metabolic syndrome is a laboratory construct without clinical significance and that no intervention is needed until he develops frank type 2 diabetes or a cardiovascular event
This approach is dangerously incorrect. Metabolic syndrome significantly increases cardiovascular disease risk (approximately 2-fold) and diabetes risk (approximately 5-fold within 5 years). It represents a critical window for primary prevention through lifestyle intervention. The Diabetes Prevention Program and other landmark studies demonstrate that intervention during the metabolic syndrome stage can prevent progression to type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular events. Dismissing metabolic syndrome as clinically insignificant and waiting for overt disease to develop represents a fundamental misunderstanding of preventive medicine principles.
(Choice E)
Refer the patient to a registered dietitian and schedule follow-up in one year to reassess metabolic syndrome criteria, as specialized nutrition counseling is more effective than brief physician intervention
While referral to a registered dietitian is an excellent and appropriate adjunct intervention, deferring all counseling to a future specialist visit and returning in one year without any physician-level guidance is not appropriate for a patient with metabolic syndrome who is motivated and asking for direction. Evidence from primary care settings demonstrates that brief physician counseling — even five minutes of specific, collaborative goal-setting — significantly improves patient adoption of lifestyle modifications compared to no counseling. The physician's role in providing immediate, actionable guidance is not replaced by specialist referral.

pages.question: A 30-week gestational age female infant is now 8 weeks old (38 weeks corrected gestational age) and is being prepared for NICU discharge. Her birth weight was 1,200 g and her current weight is 2,050 g, which is below the 10th percentile for corrected age. She has been tolerating full enteral feeds via bottle with pasteurized donor human milk fortified with human milk fortifier. The team is counseling the mother about nutritional supplementation after discharge. Which of the following micronutrient supplementation regimens is most appropriate for this infant at discharge?

answers.text:
Vitamin D 200 IU/day only; iron and folate are adequate from fortified donor milk
(100%)

Iron 2–4 mg/kg/day, vitamin D 400–1,000 IU/day, and folate supplementation
(0%)

Iron 1 mg/kg/day only; vitamin D and folate synthesis is adequate at term-equivalent age
(0%)

Calcium and phosphorus supplementation only, to prevent metabolic bone disease
(0%)

No supplementation needed; preterm discharge formula provides adequate micronutrients
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Preterm infants require supplementation with iron (2–4 mg/kg/day), vitamin D (400–1,000 IU/day), and folate after discharge to prevent deficiency states including iron-deficiency anemia, rickets, and megaloblastic anemia. These supplements are needed because preterm infants miss the third-trimester accumulation of micronutrients and have accelerated growth demands that cannot be met by diet alone in the early months of life.
(Choice A)
Vitamin D 200 IU/day only; iron and folate are adequate from fortified donor milk
While human milk fortifier provides some micronutrients during NICU stay, it is typically discontinued at discharge. A vitamin D dose of 200 IU/day is insufficient for preterm infants, who require 400-1,000 IU/day due to limited stores and high bone mineralization demands. Additionally, preterm infants are born with substantially depleted iron stores because 80% of fetal iron transfer occurs in the third trimester, which they missed. Without dedicated iron supplementation at 2-4 mg/kg/day, this infant faces high risk for iron-deficiency anemia during rapid post-discharge growth.
(Choice B)
Iron 2–4 mg/kg/day, vitamin D 400–1,000 IU/day, and folate supplementation
Preterm infants are born with significantly reduced iron stores because approximately 80% of fetal iron is transferred from the placenta during the third trimester, which preterm infants miss. Iron supplementation at 2–4 mg/kg/day beginning by 2–4 weeks of age and continued through 12 months corrected age is recommended to prevent iron-deficiency anemia during the rapid growth period. Vitamin D supplementation at 400–1,000 IU/day is required because preterm infants have limited stores, reduced skin synthesis, and high bone mineralization demands; deficiency leads to metabolic bone disease of prematurity (rickets). Folate is also recommended because preterm infants have high cell turnover and growth demands that may outpace dietary intake, placing them at risk for megaloblastic anemia. Human milk alone, even fortified, does not reliably meet all of these needs post-discharge, making a combined supplement regimen standard of care.
(Choice C)
Iron 1 mg/kg/day only; vitamin D and folate synthesis is adequate at term-equivalent age
Although this infant has reached 38 weeks corrected age, preterm infants continue to require vitamin D supplementation regardless of corrected gestational age at discharge. They have limited vitamin D stores from birth and reduced cutaneous synthesis capacity, especially with typical limited sun exposure. The proposed iron dose of 1 mg/kg/day is insufficient; preterm infants require 2-4 mg/kg/day due to their substantially depleted iron stores from missing third-trimester placental iron transfer. Folate supplementation is also necessary given the high cell turnover and rapid growth demands that characterize the post-discharge period.
(Choice D)
Calcium and phosphorus supplementation only, to prevent metabolic bone disease
Calcium and phosphorus supplementation is important during the NICU stay for very preterm infants, but by discharge, a well-growing preterm infant on fortified feeds or preterm discharge formula typically has improving bone mineralization. Focusing solely on calcium and phosphorus while omitting iron and vitamin D would leave the infant at risk for iron-deficiency anemia and rickets. A comprehensive micronutrient supplementation approach including iron, vitamin D, and folate is the evidence-based standard at discharge.
(Choice E)
No supplementation needed; preterm discharge formula provides adequate micronutrients
Although preterm discharge formulas contain higher levels of protein, calcium, and phosphorus compared to standard term formulas, they do not provide adequate iron, vitamin D, and folate to meet the specialized needs of growth-restricted preterm infants. Supplementation recommendations are based on the infant's degree of prematurity and current growth status, not formula composition alone. For this infant born at 30 weeks with current weight below the 10th percentile, relying solely on formula without additional micronutrient supplementation would create significant risk for iron-deficiency anemia and vitamin D deficiency.

pages.question:
A 72-year-old man residing in a nursing home presents with acute onset of confusion, fever, and foul-smelling urine. He has a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and chronic urinary retention managed with intermittent self-catheterization. Urinalysis is shown below. Which of the following dipstick findings is most likely in this patient?



White blood cell count	7400/mm³
Neutrophils	60%
Lymphocytes	30%
Monocytes	7%
Eosinophils	2%
Basophils	1%
Red blood cell count	4.7x10^6/µL
Hemoglobin	14.0 g/dL
Hematocrit	42%
Platelet count	255000/µL
Mean platelet volume	9.6 fL
Urine color	Yellow
Urine appearance	Clear
Specific gravity	1.015
Urine pH	6.0
Urine protein	Negative
Urine glucose	Negative
Urine ketones	Negative
Urine blood	Negative
Leukocyte esterase	Negative
Nitrites	Negative
Urine red blood cells	0-2/hpf
Urine white blood cells	0-2/hpf
Urine casts	None seen
Urine bacteria	None seen

answers.text:
Negative nitrites and negative leukocyte esterase
(36.54%)

Negative nitrites and positive leukocyte esterase
(0%)

Positive nitrites and positive leukocyte esterase
(61.54%)

Positive nitrites and negative leukocyte esterase
(1.92%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
In this elderly patient with symptoms suggestive of a urinary tract infection caused by Enterobacteriaceae, the urine dipstick is expected to be positive for both nitrites (indicating gram-negative bacteria) and leukocyte esterase (indicating pyuria).
(Choice A)
Negative nitrites and negative leukocyte esterase
This is incorrect. In a symptomatic UTI with bacteriuria, both nitrites and esterase are typically positive when caused by Enterobacteriaceae.
(Choice B)
Negative nitrites and positive leukocyte esterase
This pattern suggests UTI caused by organisms that don't reduce nitrates (such as Enterococcus, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, or Pseudomonas). However, in elderly nursing home patients, Enterobacteriaceae (which do reduce nitrates) are the most common cause.
(Choice C)
Positive nitrites and positive leukocyte esterase
This is correct. The presence of nitrites indicates nitrate-reducing bacteria like Enterobacteriaceae (e.g., E. coli), and positive leukocyte esterase reflects pyuria due to inflammation from the infection.
(Choice D)
Positive nitrites and negative leukocyte esterase
This combination is uncommon but possible in early UTI or if the bacterial load is insufficient to produce significant pyuria. However, given the strong clinical presentation, both markers would typically be positive.

pages.question:
A 62-year-old man with a history of childhood neck irradiation for thymic enlargement presents with palpitations, anxiety, and a 15-pound weight loss over the past 4 months. He denies eye symptoms or family history of thyroid disease. Examination reveals tachycardia and a firm, solitary nodule in the left thyroid lobe without diffuse enlargement. Lab values are shown below. A radioactive iodine uptake scan demonstrates intense focal uptake in the left lobe nodule with suppression of uptake in the remainder of the gland. What is the underlying mechanism causing this patient's hyperthyroidism?



Hemoglobin	13.6 g/dL
Hematocrit	41 %
WBC	7.0 x10^3/µL
Neutrophils	55 %
Lymphocytes	30 %
Monocytes	5 %
Eosinophils	2 %
Platelets	270 x10^3/µL
MCV	89 fL
AST	25 U/L
ALT	28 U/L
Alkaline Phosphatase	90 U/L
Total Bilirubin	0.8 mg/dL
Albumin	4.2 g/dL
Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH)	<0.01 mU/L
Free T4	3.5 ng/dL
Free T3	220 ng/dL

answers.text:
Destructive release of preformed thyroid hormone
(19.15%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has hyperthyroidism due to a toxic adenoma (hot nodule), characterized by a solitary area of intense radioiodine uptake with suppression of the surrounding thyroid tissue, suppressed TSH, and elevated thyroid hormones. This condition arises from autonomous thyroid hormone production due to activating somatic mutations in the TSH receptor or G-protein signaling pathway, leading to constitutive cAMP-mediated hormone synthesis and secretion independent of TSH stimulation. The history of childhood neck irradiation is a known risk factor for thyroid nodule development.
(Choice A)
Autonomous thyroid hormone production
Toxic adenomas produce thyroid hormones independently of TSH due to somatic mutations causing constitutive activation of signaling pathways, leading to focal hyperfunction seen on scan.
(Choice B)
Pituitary overproduction of TSH
TSH-secreting pituitary adenomas cause secondary (central) hyperthyroidism with paradoxically elevated or inappropriately normal TSH levels despite high thyroid hormones. This patient has suppressed TSH (<0.01 mU/L), indicating primary thyroid pathology, not pituitary overproduction.
(Choice C)
Multiple areas of nodular autonomy
This describes toxic multinodular goiter (Plummer disease), which presents with multiple autonomously functioning nodules showing patchy increased uptake in several areas on radioiodine scan. This patient has a single hot nodule with suppression of the remaining thyroid tissue, consistent with a solitary toxic adenoma.
(Choice D)
Antibody-mediated TSH receptor stimulation
This describes Graves disease, which is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that mimic TSH action. Graves disease typically presents with diffuse thyroid enlargement and diffuse uptake on radioiodine scan, contrasting with the solitary nodular uptake pattern seen in this patient.
(Choice E)
Destructive release of preformed thyroid hormone
This mechanism occurs in thyroiditis (subacute, postpartum, or drug-induced), where inflammation causes release of preformed thyroid hormones from damaged follicles. These conditions show low or absent radioiodine uptake due to impaired iodine organification, contrasting with the intense focal uptake in this case.

pages.question:
A 28-year-old woman with a history of bulimia nervosa presents to the clinic complaining of severe muscle weakness, fatigue, and intermittent cramps in her legs that have worsened over the past week. She admits to frequent self-induced vomiting after binge eating episodes. Physical examination reveals generalized muscle weakness, particularly in the proximal muscles, with normal deep tendon reflexes and no sensory deficits. Laboratory tests are shown below. An electrocardiogram is obtained. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?



WBC	7.8 x10^3/µL
Neutrophils	60 %
Lymphocytes	30 %
Monocytes	6 %
Eosinophils	3 %
Basophils	1 %
RBC	4.7 x10^6/µL
Hemoglobin	13.8 g/dL
Hematocrit	41 %
MCV	88 fL
MCH	29 pg
MCHC	34 g/dL
RDW	12.8 %
Platelets	260 x10^3/µL
Sodium	139 mEq/L
Potassium	2.8 mEq/L
Chloride	102 mEq/L
BUN	12 mg/dL
Creatinine	0.9 mg/dL
Glucose	92 mg/dL
Calcium	9.2 mg/dL
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This woman has weakness due to hypokalemia (K+ 2.8 mEq/L) caused by recurrent vomiting associated with bulimia nervosa. Hypokalemia impairs muscle membrane excitability, causing weakness, fatigue, and cramps. Severe hypokalemia can also cause cardiac arrhythmias with ECG changes including U waves, flattened T waves, and ST depression. The normal reflexes and absence of focal neurological deficits exclude other neuromuscular conditions.
(Choice A)
Spinal stenosis
Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication with back and leg pain that worsens with walking and improves with sitting or leaning forward. It doesn't cause generalized proximal weakness or relate to metabolic disturbances from vomiting.
(Choice B)
Electrolyte disturbance
Hypokalemia from recurrent vomiting can cause muscle weakness and cramps by disrupting normal neuromuscular function and membrane potentials.
(Choice C)
Guillain-Barré syndrome
Guillain-Barré syndrome presents with ascending paralysis, areflexia, and often follows infection, without association to bulimia or low potassium.
(Choice D)
Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis typically presents with focal neurological deficits, visual disturbances, or sensory changes that come and go over time, not generalized symmetric weakness with normal reflexes directly related to vomiting episodes.
(Choice E)
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism can cause fatigue and proximal weakness, but develops gradually over months with additional symptoms like weight gain, cold intolerance, and bradycardia. The acute presentation and severe hypokalemia point to a different etiology.

pages.question: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of left-sided weakness, facial droop, and expressive aphasia. He reports that 48 hours earlier, he was involved in a motor vehicle accident where he was ejected from the car and sustained a penetrating injury to the posterior oropharynx from a broken piece of metal debris. Initial evaluation at that time showed a laceration in the soft palate, which was sutured, and he was discharged. Vital signs are currently normal, and neurologic examination confirms left hemiparesis, left facial weakness, and difficulty forming words. CT head without contrast is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's symptoms of hemiparesis, facial droop, and expressive aphasia occurring 48 hours after penetrating injury to the posterior oropharynx suggest internal carotid artery dissection. The proximity of the internal carotid artery to the posterior oropharynx makes it vulnerable to injury from penetrating trauma, leading to vessel wall dissection, thrombus formation, and subsequent embolic or hypoperfusion stroke in the anterior circulation territory. The delayed presentation is characteristic of post-traumatic arterial dissection. Other choices are inconsistent with the specific anatomical relationship and clinical presentation pattern.
(Choice A)
Cerebral contusion
Cerebral contusion from direct head trauma would likely show abnormalities on CT head and would have presented immediately after the accident, not with delayed focal neurologic symptoms 48 hours later after isolated oropharyngeal injury without head impact.
(Choice B)
Carotid artery dissection
Trauma to the posterior oropharynx can directly injure the internal carotid artery, leading to dissection and subsequent thromboembolism or ischemia, causing stroke-like symptoms such as hemiparesis and aphasia.
(Choice C)
Vertebral artery dissection
Vertebral artery dissection typically presents with posterior circulation symptoms like vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, or Wallenberg syndrome, not anterior circulation deficits like hemiparesis and expressive aphasia which indicate middle cerebral artery territory involvement.
(Choice D)
Transient ischemic attack
While the neurologic symptoms could resemble a TIA, the persistent nature of the deficits beyond the typical TIA timeframe and the clear history of penetrating oropharyngeal trauma point to a structural vascular injury like carotid dissection rather than a transient ischemic event.
(Choice E)
Retropharyngeal abscess
A retropharyngeal abscess could develop after oropharyngeal trauma but would typically present with fever, severe neck pain, dysphagia, trismus, and possibly airway compromise, not acute focal neurologic deficits like hemiparesis and aphasia.

pages.question: A 32-year-old woman is rushed to the trauma unit following a high-speed motorcycle accident. Upon examination, she appears acutely ill. Her blood pressure is recorded at 86/44 mmHg, with a heart rate of 130/min and respiration rate of 26/min. Upon physical examination, collapsed neck veins are noted. She presents with equal breath sounds bilaterally, normal heart sounds, and an unchanged trachea position. She is only intermittently responsive, but her pupils are equal and reactive. No overt head trauma is observed. There is notable abdominal swelling, with tenderness and muscular guarding across all quadrants. After the patient's airway is secured and initial resuscitation is performed, what should the next step in her management be?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient presents with hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia) and clinical signs of intra-abdominal injury (abdominal distension, tenderness, and guarding across all quadrants) following blunt trauma. These findings indicate probable intraperitoneal hemorrhage requiring immediate surgical control. In hemodynamically unstable trauma patients with clear clinical evidence of significant intra-abdominal injury, exploratory laparotomy should be performed without delay. Diagnostic studies like FAST or CT are appropriate for stable patients but should not delay definitive surgical management in unstable patients with obvious peritoneal signs.
(Choice A)
Focused Abdominal Sonography for Trauma
FAST is an excellent initial assessment tool for detecting free fluid in trauma patients, but in hemodynamically unstable patients with clear clinical signs of intra-abdominal injury (hypotension, tachycardia, abdominal tenderness with guarding), surgical intervention should not be delayed for additional diagnostic procedures.
(Choice B)
Abdominal CT scan
CT scans are more appropriate for stable patients, whereas unstable patients warrant direct surgical intervention.
(Choice C)
Nasogastric decompression
Nasogastric decompression may be performed as part of surgical preparation, but it does not address the underlying cause of hemodynamic instability from suspected intra-abdominal hemorrhage requiring immediate surgical control.
(Choice D)
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage
While DPL can detect intraperitoneal bleeding, it is rarely used in modern trauma management when clinical findings clearly indicate the need for surgical intervention, as in this hemodynamically unstable patient with obvious peritoneal signs.
(Choice E)
Exploratory laparotomy
This procedure is critical for swiftly identifying and managing intra-abdominal injuries due to blunt trauma and potential peritoneal irritation or instability.

pages.question: A mother brings her 3-year-old son to the pediatrician for a well-child visit. The child's BMI is at the 88th percentile. The mother reports that he drinks approximately 12 oz of apple juice, 8 oz of a fruit punch drink, and 8 oz of whole milk daily. He rarely drinks plain water. His dentist recently noted early enamel demineralization on his upper front teeth. The mother asks for guidance on improving his beverage choices. Which of the following recommendations is most consistent with current evidence-based beverage guidelines for young children?

answers.text:
Advise the mother to eliminate the fruit punch drink entirely, reduce 100% apple juice to no more than 4 oz per day, and make water the primary beverage throughout the day.
(100%)

Replace the fruit punch with additional 100% fruit juice, as 100% juice is always preferable to fruit drinks for children.
(0%)

Recommend adding a daily multivitamin so the child can continue his current beverage pattern without nutritional concerns.
(0%)

Switch all beverages to low-fat milk, as dairy provides complete nutrition for toddlers and should be their primary beverage.
(0%)

Continue the current juice intake since 100% apple juice provides vitamins C and potassium beneficial for toddler growth.
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
For children ages 2-3, current guidelines recommend limiting 100% fruit juice to no more than 4 oz per day and eliminating fruit-flavored drinks, which are sugar-sweetened beverages with no nutritional benefit. Water should be the primary beverage, and dental caries and excessive caloric intake are well-documented consequences of high juice and SSB consumption in early childhood. Whole milk in appropriate amounts remains appropriate for toddlers over age 2, though low-fat options may be considered.
(Choice A)
Advise the mother to eliminate the fruit punch drink entirely, reduce 100% apple juice to no more than 4 oz per day, and make water the primary beverage throughout the day.
Fruit punch and other fruit-flavored drinks are sugar-sweetened beverages that provide little to no nutritional value and are strongly associated with dental caries, obesity, and excess caloric intake in children. Current AAP and Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommendations state that children ages 1-3 should consume no more than 4 oz of 100% fruit juice per day, and that water should be the primary beverage. This child is consuming 12 oz of juice and 8 oz of a fruit-flavored SSB daily, which together contribute significantly to his elevated BMI and early dental enamel breakdown. Eliminating the fruit punch entirely and reducing juice to 4 oz per day while promoting water as the primary beverage addresses both excess caloric intake and dental health concerns. Encouraging families to offer water freely and limit juice by using smaller cups and diluting juice during the transition are practical strategies. Whole milk at 8 oz per day for a toddler is within acceptable range after age 2, though low-fat milk becomes appropriate at age 2 if excess weight is a concern.
(Choice B)
Replace the fruit punch with additional 100% fruit juice, as 100% juice is always preferable to fruit drinks for children.
While 100% fruit juice is nutritionally superior to sugar-sweetened fruit drinks, this recommendation would worsen the problem. The child is already consuming 12 oz of 100% apple juice daily, which is three times the AAP-recommended maximum of 4 oz per day for ages 1-3 years. Replacing the 8 oz fruit punch with additional juice would increase total juice intake to 20 oz daily, further exacerbating the caloric excess contributing to his elevated BMI and dental demineralization.
(Choice C)
Recommend adding a daily multivitamin so the child can continue his current beverage pattern without nutritional concerns.
A multivitamin does not address the excess sugar intake, caloric contribution to elevated BMI, or dental harm associated with this child's current beverage pattern. The problem is not a nutritional deficiency that can be supplemented — it is excess sugar consumption from SSBs and excessive juice intake driving overweight and dental demineralization. Behavioral change in beverage selection is the appropriate intervention.
(Choice D)
Switch all beverages to low-fat milk, as dairy provides complete nutrition for toddlers and should be their primary beverage.
While milk is nutritionally valuable for toddlers, it should not replace water as the primary beverage. The AAP recommends 16-24 oz of milk per day for toddlers, but water should remain the main source of hydration. Excessive milk intake can contribute to excess calories and may displace other important nutrients from solid foods. This approach fails to address the core issues: eliminating sugar-sweetened beverages and reducing total juice intake to recommended levels.
(Choice E)
Continue the current juice intake since 100% apple juice provides vitamins C and potassium beneficial for toddler growth.
While 100% apple juice does contain vitamins C and potassium, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends limiting 100% fruit juice to no more than 4 oz per day for children ages 1-3 years due to high sugar content and lack of fiber compared to whole fruit. This child is consuming 12 oz daily (three times the recommended limit), which contributes to his elevated BMI (88th percentile) and early dental enamel demineralization. The modest nutritional benefits do not outweigh the risks of excess sugar intake at this volume.

pages.question: A 35-year-old woman presents to the clinic with her partner, who believes she is exaggerating her symptoms and avoiding responsibilities. She has been experiencing intermittent episodes of vision disturbances, unilateral weakness, and numbness for the past year. Recently, she reported experiencing double vision and impaired bladder control. Interestingly, her symptoms improve during her vacation. She appears to be in no distress and her neurological examination is unrevealing. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test to confirm the suspected medical condition?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This case reflects a typical presentation of multiple sclerosis (MS), characterized by relapsing-remitting neurological symptoms in a young adult. The key features include dissemination in space (multiple neurological symptoms affecting different areas) and time (symptoms occurring over the past year with remissions). Brain MRI is the gold standard initial diagnostic test as it can demonstrate characteristic T2 hyperintense lesions in periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial regions consistent with demyelination, fulfilling the 2017 McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis.
(Choice A)
Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis
While CSF analysis can show oligoclonal bands and elevated IgG index in MS patients, it is not the first-line diagnostic test. The 2017 McDonald criteria prioritize MRI findings for MS diagnosis, with CSF analysis reserved for cases where MRI findings are equivocal or atypical.
(Choice B)
EEG
EEG measures electrical activity in the brain and is primarily used to diagnose seizure disorders. MS does not cause characteristic EEG changes, making this test irrelevant for diagnosing demyelinating disease.
(Choice C)
Visual Field Test
Visual field testing assesses peripheral vision defects but cannot identify the underlying cause of visual disturbances. While MS can cause visual field defects, this test doesn't reveal demyelinating lesions needed for diagnosis.
(Choice D)
Brain MRI
An MRI of the brain is pivotal in diagnosing multiple sclerosis as it can reveal characteristic lesions indicative of demyelination.
(Choice E)
CBC with differential
CBC with differential is a general screening blood test that cannot detect demyelinating lesions or confirm MS diagnosis. While it may be ordered to rule out other conditions, it provides no specific information about multiple sclerosis.

pages.question: A 48-year-old female teacher presents to the clinic after experiencing a sudden 'pop' and sharp pain in her right calf while running across the schoolyard to assist a student. She now has difficulty bearing weight on the right leg and notices swelling around the posterior ankle. On physical examination, there is ecchymosis, a palpable gap in the Achilles tendon region, and weak active plantar flexion of the right foot. However, when the calf squeeze test is performed, there is no passive plantar flexion of the foot. This patient's injury is most likely to impair her ability to perform which of the following actions?

answers.text:
Everting the right foot against resistance
(0%)

Dorsiflexing the right ankle against resistance
(7.25%)

Walking on tiptoes with the right foot
(86.96%)

Walking on heels with the right foot
(4.35%)

Inverting the right foot against resistance
(1.45%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has sudden sharp pain in the right calf with a 'pop' sensation, palpable gap, and positive calf squeeze/Thompson test (absent passive plantar flexion), indicating Achilles tendon rupture. Active plantar flexion is preserved due to accessory muscles, but walking on tiptoes is impaired due to loss of gastrocnemius and soleus function. Other ankle motions controlled by different muscles are not significantly impaired.
(Choice A)
Everting the right foot against resistance
Foot eversion is primarily controlled by the fibularis (peroneus) longus and brevis muscles, which are innervated by the superficial fibular (peroneal) nerve. These muscles have separate anatomical pathways from the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles affected by Achilles tendon rupture, so eversion function remains preserved.
(Choice B)
Dorsiflexing the right ankle against resistance
Dorsiflexion against resistance is primarily controlled by the tibialis anterior muscle and other dorsiflexors (extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus) innervated by the deep peroneal nerve. The Achilles tendon rupture affects plantar flexion muscles (gastrocnemius and soleus) but leaves the dorsiflexor compartment intact.
(Choice C)
Walking on tiptoes with the right foot
Achilles tendon rupture impairs the function of the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, which are essential for pushing off and standing on tiptoes. This ability is significantly affected despite preserved weak active plantar flexion from accessory muscles like the tibialis posterior and toe flexors.
(Choice D)
Walking on heels with the right foot
Walking on heels requires dorsiflexion, which is primarily controlled by the tibialis anterior muscle and other dorsiflexors innervated by the deep peroneal nerve. Since the Achilles tendon connects the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles to the calcaneus for plantar flexion, its rupture does not affect the dorsiflexor muscles or heel walking ability.
(Choice E)
Inverting the right foot against resistance
Foot inversion is primarily performed by the tibialis posterior muscle (with assistance from tibialis anterior and flexor digitorum longus). Since these muscles have separate tendons and anatomical pathways from the Achilles tendon, inversion strength remains unaffected by Achilles tendon rupture.

pages.question: A 34-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted for medically supervised nutritional rehabilitation after losing 18% of her body weight over six months. On admission, her serum phosphorus is 3.1 mg/dL, potassium is 3.6 mEq/L, and magnesium is 1.8 mg/dL. She is started on a gradual enteral feeding protocol at 20 kcal/kg/day. On hospital day 3, she becomes confused and develops new-onset muscle weakness and shortness of breath. Repeat laboratory values show serum phosphorus 1.4 mg/dL, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, and magnesium 1.5 mg/dL. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia without other abnormalities. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiologic mechanism responsible for her hypophosphatemia?

answers.text:
Malabsorption of phosphorus secondary to intestinal villous atrophy from chronic undernutrition
(20%)

Excessive urinary phosphorus wasting caused by osmotic diuresis from glucosuria after caloric reintroduction
(0%)

Increased renal phosphorus excretion secondary to elevated parathyroid hormone levels from chronic malnutrition
(0%)

Depletion of phosphorus stores through consumption as a cofactor for insulin receptor phosphorylation in peripheral tissues
(0%)

Carbohydrate reintroduction stimulates insulin secretion, driving intracellular uptake of phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium and depleting serum levels
(80%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate reintroduction after prolonged starvation triggers insulin secretion, driving glucose, phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium into cells. The resultant hypophosphatemia can cause life-threatening complications including respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmias, hemolytic anemia, and neurologic dysfunction. Gradual caloric reintroduction with close electrolyte monitoring and prophylactic phosphorus supplementation are essential to prevent this syndrome.
(Choice A)
Malabsorption of phosphorus secondary to intestinal villous atrophy from chronic undernutrition
Intestinal villous atrophy can occur in severe malnutrition and may reduce absorption of multiple nutrients; however, this does not explain the acute drop in serum phosphorus that occurred specifically after feeding was initiated in this patient. If malabsorption were the primary mechanism, one would not expect a precipitous decline in phosphorus triggered by the introduction of feeding. The temporal relationship strongly favors an intracellular shift mechanism rather than a gastrointestinal absorptive defect.
(Choice B)
Excessive urinary phosphorus wasting caused by osmotic diuresis from glucosuria after caloric reintroduction
Osmotic diuresis from glucosuria requires significant hyperglycemia (typically >180 mg/dL) to exceed the renal threshold for glucose reabsorption, which is not described in this patient. Moreover, this patient has anorexia nervosa without diabetes, making significant glucosuria unlikely. While osmotic diuresis can theoretically cause phosphaturia, the primary mechanism of hypophosphatemia in refeeding syndrome is insulin-mediated intracellular shift of phosphorus, not renal wasting.
(Choice C)
Increased renal phosphorus excretion secondary to elevated parathyroid hormone levels from chronic malnutrition
While secondary hyperparathyroidism can occur in chronic malnutrition and cause phosphaturia, this is not the primary mechanism of hypophosphatemia in refeeding syndrome. The key clinical clue is the timing—the acute drop in serum phosphorus occurred specifically after feeding commenced on hospital day 3, not as a gradual process during the starvation phase. This temporal relationship points to refeeding physiology (intracellular shift) rather than a chronic hormonal mechanism causing renal wasting.
(Choice D)
Depletion of phosphorus stores through consumption as a cofactor for insulin receptor phosphorylation in peripheral tissues
While phosphorus is essential for numerous enzymatic reactions including those involved in insulin signaling, depletion of serum phosphorus in refeeding syndrome is primarily explained by bulk intracellular shift driven by insulin-mediated cellular uptake and increased demand for phosphorus in glycolysis and ATP synthesis—not by a specific consumption as a cofactor for insulin receptor phosphorylation. This explanation misattributes the mechanism to a minor biochemical role rather than the dominant physiologic shift.
(Choice E)
Carbohydrate reintroduction stimulates insulin secretion, driving intracellular uptake of phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium and depleting serum levels
During prolonged starvation, total body phosphorus stores become significantly depleted even when serum phosphorus may appear near-normal due to transcellular shifts. When carbohydrates are reintroduced, insulin is secreted in response to the glucose load and stimulates cellular uptake of glucose, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus for anabolic processes including glycolysis, ATP synthesis, and protein synthesis. This rapid intracellular shift causes acute drops in serum phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium—collectively defining refeeding syndrome. Hypophosphatemia is the hallmark electrolyte abnormality and can cause impaired ATP production, leading to widespread organ dysfunction including respiratory muscle weakness (risking respiratory failure), cardiac arrhythmias, hemolytic anemia (due to impaired red cell membrane integrity), and neurologic manifestations such as confusion and weakness. Management involves cautious caloric reintroduction (typically 10–20 kcal/kg/day initially), frequent electrolyte monitoring, and phosphorus supplementation when levels fall below safe thresholds.

pages.question: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia undergoes elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Two days postoperatively, while recovering in the hospital, he develops sudden-onset right-sided hemiparesis, facial droop, and expressive aphasia at 10:00 AM. It is now 11:00 AM. His blood pressure is 165/90 mm Hg, and his National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score is 16. Noncontrast head CT shows no evidence of hemorrhage, and CT angiography reveals an occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery. Which of the following is the most appropriate acute treatment for this patient?

answers.text:
Intravenous alteplase followed by mechanical thrombectomy
(24.64%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has an acute ischemic stroke with large vessel occlusion presenting 1 hour after symptom onset, which is within the time window for both intravenous thrombolysis (<4.5 hours) and mechanical thrombectomy (<24 hours). However, his recent major surgery (cholecystectomy 2 days ago) is an absolute contraindication for thrombolysis due to bleeding risk. Eligibility for thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy is assessed independently, so he remains eligible for mechanical thrombectomy alone. This case illustrates the importance of recognizing contraindications to thrombolysis while understanding that mechanical thrombectomy may still be appropriate.
(Choice A)
Aspirin and high-intensity statin therapy
Incorrect. While antiplatelet and statin therapy are essential components of secondary stroke prevention, this patient requires immediate reperfusion therapy for his acute large vessel occlusion. Medical management alone would be inappropriate when mechanical thrombectomy is indicated and available within the therapeutic window.
(Choice B)
Intravenous alteplase
Incorrect. Recent major surgery within 14 days is an absolute contraindication for intravenous alteplase due to significantly increased risk of surgical site bleeding. This patient requires immediate reperfusion therapy with mechanical thrombectomy, not delayed medical management.
(Choice C)
Intravenous alteplase followed by mechanical thrombectomy
Incorrect. While this patient presents within the time window for both therapies (1 hour from onset), recent major surgery within 14 days is an absolute contraindication for intravenous alteplase due to significantly increased risk of surgical site bleeding. Mechanical thrombectomy eligibility is assessed independently and is not contraindicated by recent surgery.
(Choice D)
Mechanical thrombectomy
Correct. The patient is not eligible for thrombolysis due to recent surgery, but eligibility is independent, and he qualifies for mechanical thrombectomy given the large vessel occlusion and presentation within 24 hours.

pages.question: A 3-day-old female infant is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of lethargy and difficulty feeding since birth. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation to a 42-year-old mother via spontaneous vaginal delivery. Pregnancy was uncomplicated, but prenatal screening was declined. On examination, the infant weighs 2.6 kg (5th percentile), has a flat occiput, epicanthal folds, a protruding tongue, and loose skin at the nape of the neck. She exhibits generalized hypotonia, a weak cry, and a single transverse crease on each palm. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This neonate presents with characteristic features of Down syndrome, including hypotonia, poor feeding, macroglossia, epicanthal folds, flat occiput, nuchal skin redundancy, single palmar creases, and a heart murmur suggestive of a congenital defect. The condition is caused by trisomy 21, confirmed by karyotype analysis.
(Choice A)
Congenital hypothyroidism
This is incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism can cause hypotonia, poor feeding, and macroglossia, but typically presents with prolonged physiologic jaundice, large posterior fontanelle, and coarse facial features. It does not cause the specific dysmorphic features seen here (epicanthal folds, flat occiput, single palmar creases) which are pathognomonic for a chromosomal disorder.
(Choice B)
Prader-Willi syndrome
This is incorrect. Prader-Willi syndrome presents with neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulties, but the characteristic facial features include almond-shaped eyes, narrow bifrontal diameter, and down-turned mouth. It lacks the epicanthal folds, protruding tongue, and single palmar creases seen in this case. It is due to deletion or imprinting defects on chromosome 15q11-q13.
(Choice C)
Trisomy 18
This is incorrect. Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) features severe intrauterine growth restriction, characteristic clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and severe congenital heart defects. While growth restriction is present in this case, the specific dysmorphic features (epicanthal folds, protruding tongue, single palmar creases) are not characteristic of Edwards syndrome.
(Choice D)
Noonan syndrome
This is incorrect. Noonan syndrome may include congenital heart defects, short stature, and webbed neck, but the characteristic facial features include prominent forehead, hypertelorism, ptosis, and low-set posteriorly rotated ears. The profound neonatal hypotonia, epicanthal folds, protruding tongue, and single palmar creases are not typical of Noonan syndrome. It is caused by mutations affecting the RAS-MAPK pathway.
(Choice E)
Down syndrome
This is the correct diagnosis. The infant's features, including hypotonia, dysmorphic facial characteristics, single palmar creases, and heart murmur, are classic for Down syndrome, which is caused by trisomy 21 in most cases.

pages.question: A 35-year-old woman experienced a sudden loss of consciousness while gardening. She is brought to the emergency department where her blood pressure reads 88/55 mm Hg, and her respiratory rate is 32/min. Physical examination reveals tracheal deviation to the right, decreased breath sounds on the left, and distended neck veins. Swelling and ecchymosis are evident over her upper left arm. Which immediate intervention would most rapidly stabilize her condition?

answers.text:
Administer high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask
(0%)

Stabilize the fractured arm with a splint
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's symptoms and presentation are classic for tension pneumothorax, a scenario in which air is trapped in the pleural cavity, causing increased intrathoracic pressure leading to decreased venous return to the heart. This results in reduced cardiac output and, if not treated immediately, can be fatal. Needle decompression is crucial for decompressing the pleura and stabilizing the patient until definitive tube thoracostomy can be performed.
(Choice A)
Perform rapid needle decompression
Needle thoracostomy is an immediate procedure that relieves pressure in the pleural cavity, crucial for treating a tension pneumothorax and restoring hemodynamic stability.
(Choice B)
Conduct an emergency tracheostomy
Emergency tracheostomy is indicated for upper airway obstruction, not for tension pneumothorax. The patient's respiratory distress is due to impaired venous return and cardiac compression from increased pleural pressure, not airway compromise. This procedure would delay life-saving decompression and is inappropriate for this clinical scenario.
(Choice C)
Initiate aggressive intravenous fluid therapy
While IV fluid therapy might temporarily support blood pressure, it will not address the underlying pathophysiology of tension pneumothorax. The hemodynamic instability is caused by impaired venous return due to increased intrathoracic pressure, not hypovolemia. Fluids could potentially worsen the situation by increasing preload against an already compressed heart.
(Choice D)
Administer high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask
High-flow oxygen may provide marginal benefit but does not address the mechanical obstruction to venous return caused by the tension pneumothorax. The patient's hypoxia and hemodynamic compromise are primarily due to impaired cardiac filling, not ventilation-perfusion mismatch, making oxygen supplementation insufficient as the primary intervention.
(Choice E)
Stabilize the fractured arm with a splint
While the arm fracture requires attention, tension pneumothorax is immediately life-threatening and takes priority in the ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) approach to trauma. The hemodynamic instability and respiratory compromise from the pneumothorax will be fatal within minutes if not addressed, whereas the fracture, though painful, is not immediately life-threatening.

pages.question:
A 14-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her foster parents for evaluation of short stature and delayed puberty. She was adopted from an orphanage abroad at age 10, and her medical history is limited, but she has had recurrent urinary tract infections and mild sensorineural hearing loss. On examination, she has a height of 140 cm (below the 3rd percentile), wide-spaced nipples, and no breast development or pubic hair. Laboratory studies are shown below. Pelvic ultrasound reveals small, streak-like ovaries. What is the most likely underlying genetic abnormality in this patient?



Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)	85 mIU/mL
Luteinizing Hormone (LH)	45 mIU/mL
Estradiol	<10 pg/mL (normal pubertal: 20-200 pg/mL).
Hemoglobin	13.2 g/dL
Hematocrit	39 %
White Blood Cell Count	7.200 /mm³
Platelet Count	270.000 /mm³
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)	88 fL
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)	30 pg
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)	34 g/dL
Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW)	13 %

answers.text:
Congenital absence of an X chromosome
(92.11%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's presentation of primary amenorrhea, lack of secondary sexual characteristics, short stature, history of recurrent UTIs and hearing loss, along with elevated FSH and LH and streak ovaries, is consistent with Turner syndrome due to monosomy X (45,X).
(Choice A)
Congenital absence of an X chromosome
Turner syndrome (45,X) involves monosomy X, leading to gonadal dysgenesis, low estrogen, elevated FSH and LH, primary amenorrhea, short stature, and associated features like recurrent UTIs due to renal anomalies and hearing loss.
(Choice B)
FMR1 gene mutation
Fragile X syndrome results from FMR1 gene mutations and typically presents with intellectual disability and behavioral issues in both sexes, but does not cause gonadal dysgenesis or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism in females.
(Choice C)
Müllerian agenesis
Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome) causes primary amenorrhea due to absent uterus and vagina, but patients have normal ovarian function, secondary sexual characteristics, normal FSH/LH/estrogen, and 46,XX karyotype.
(Choice D)
Trisomy 21
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) causes short stature and intellectual disability but does not cause gonadal dysgenesis, primary amenorrhea, or the hypergonadotropic hypogonadism seen in this patient.
(Choice E)
47,XXY karyotype
47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) affects phenotypic males, causing hypogonadism and tall stature. This patient is phenotypically female with short stature and streak ovaries, which is incompatible with Klinefelter syndrome.

pages.question: A 68-year-old woman presents to the clinic with persistent fever and a productive cough that started five days ago. Her sputum is greenish-yellow. Accompanying symptoms include shortness of breath and mild confusion. Her background includes hypertension and chronic kidney disease. She is adherent to her medications, which include lisinopril and furosemide. She has not received any flu or pneumonia vaccinations this year. On examination, she appears flushed and mildly diaphoretic. Her vital signs show a temperature of 39.1 C (102.4 F), blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, pulse 115/min, and respirations 30/min with an oxygen saturation of 86% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals crepitations and increased breath sounds over the left lung base. A chest x-ray shows consolidation in the left lower zone. What is the next best step in management for this patient?

answers.text:
Immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
(9.21%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This case presents severe community-acquired pneumonia with life-threatening hypoxemia (O2 sat 86%). The most immediate priority is addressing hypoxemia with supplemental oxygen therapy. Concurrent IV antibiotic therapy is also essential for treating the underlying bacterial infection. Patients with chronic kidney disease are at higher risk for pneumonia complications, making prompt treatment crucial.
(Choice A)
Intravenous fluid resuscitation
Incorrect. While IV fluid resuscitation may be needed for hypotension (BP 100/60), addressing the life-threatening hypoxemia (O2 sat 86%) takes priority in the immediate management of this patient.
(Choice B)
Bronchodilator administration
Incorrect. Bronchodilators are primarily indicated for obstructive airway diseases (asthma, COPD). This patient presents with consolidative pneumonia without evidence of bronchospasm or airway obstruction.
(Choice C)
Initiation of intravenous antibiotics
IV antibiotics are essential in this patient with severe CAP and should be initiated promptly after blood cultures are drawn. However, with an O2 saturation of 86%, correcting life-threatening hypoxemia with supplemental oxygen takes immediate priority. Antibiotic therapy, while critical, acts over hours rather than seconds — making oxygen the single most appropriate next step. A beta-lactam plus macrolide combination (or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy) is the preferred regimen for hospitalized severe CAP, adjusted for CKD.
(Choice D)
Supplemental oxygen therapy
This patient has life-threatening hypoxemia with O2 saturation of 86%, which is the most immediately dangerous abnormality requiring correction within seconds to minutes. Supplemental oxygen via non-rebreather mask is the first priority in severe CAP management. While IV antibiotics are essential and should be initiated concurrently, oxygen addresses the immediate threat to life. Failure to correct hypoxemia rapidly can result in respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and death.
(Choice E)
Immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
Incorrect. While this patient has significant hypoxemia (O2 sat 86%), intubation is not the first-line intervention. Supplemental oxygen should be attempted first, with intubation reserved for cases where oxygen therapy fails to improve oxygenation or if respiratory failure progresses.

pages.question: A 65-year-old woman with a history of atrial fibrillation (not on anticoagulation) and hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset vertigo, severe occipital headache, nausea, and difficulty walking that began 2.5 hours ago. She denies hearing loss or tinnitus. On examination, her blood pressure is 180/95 mm Hg, and she has horizontal nystagmus, right-sided dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, and an ataxic gait. Noncontrast head CT shows no evidence of hemorrhage or acute infarction. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has sudden-onset, persistent vertigo with headache, dysmetria, ataxia, and nystagmus, suggestive of posterior circulation ischemia (eg, cerebellar stroke) likely due to cardioembolism from atrial fibrillation. As symptoms began within 4.5 hours and head CT rules out hemorrhage, intravenous alteplase is indicated for eligible patients with suspected ischemic stroke, regardless of the absence of hemiparesis or aphasia. Other options like meclizine or Epley maneuver are for peripheral vertigo, which does not explain the neurologic deficits. MRI, while useful, would delay thrombolysis.
(Choice A)
Administer oral meclizine
Meclizine is used for symptomatic relief in peripheral vestibular disorders (eg, vestibular neuritis, Meniere's disease), but this patient's combination of sudden onset, severe headache, dysmetria, and ataxic gait indicates central nervous system pathology requiring urgent stroke treatment, not symptomatic management.
(Choice B)
Perform Epley maneuver
The Epley maneuver treats benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), which causes brief episodes of vertigo triggered by specific head movements. This patient's continuous symptoms, severe headache, and cerebellar signs (dysmetria, ataxia) are inconsistent with BPPV and suggest acute stroke.
(Choice C)
Obtain brain MRI
While MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is more sensitive than CT for detecting acute posterior circulation infarcts, obtaining MRI would delay time-sensitive thrombolytic therapy. In this patient with high clinical suspicion for stroke and no contraindications after CT, treatment should not be delayed for advanced imaging.
(Choice D)
Administer intravenous diazepam
Diazepam may provide symptomatic relief for vertigo and could potentially help with acute vestibular symptoms, but it would be inappropriate here as it does not address the underlying stroke pathophysiology and could worsen ataxia or mask important neurological findings during the acute evaluation period.
(Choice E)
Administer intravenous alteplase
This is the correct management for suspected acute ischemic stroke in the posterior circulation within the thrombolysis window, after ruling out hemorrhage on CT.

pages.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the clinic with progressive fatigue, recurrent nosebleeds, and a recent episode of pneumonia that required hospitalization. She reports no significant travel history, but she recently started a new medication for acne. Physical examination reveals pale conjunctivae, petechiae on her lower extremities, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies are shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?



Hemoglobin	7.2 g/dL
Hematocrit	22%
Red Blood Cell Count	2.8 million/μL
Mean Corpuscular Volume	78 fL
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin	25 pg
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration	32 g/dL
Red Cell Distribution Width	18%
White Blood Cell Count	1.8 x10^9/L
Neutrophils	40%
Lymphocytes	50%
Monocytes	8%
Eosinophils	2%
Basophils	0%
Platelet Count	15 x10^9/L
Reticulocyte Count	0.3%
Serum Creatinine	0.9 mg/dL
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient exhibits pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia) with a markedly low reticulocyte count despite severe anemia, indicating inadequate bone marrow response. The absence of splenomegaly and recent acne medication use suggest drug-induced aplastic anemia as a likely cause. Bone marrow biopsy and aspiration are essential to confirm hypocellularity and establish the diagnosis before initiating treatment.
(Choice A)
Splenectomy
Splenectomy is not indicated as there is no splenomegaly on physical exam and the pancytopenia is due to bone marrow failure rather than peripheral destruction or sequestration.
(Choice B)
Red blood cell transfusion
While RBC transfusion may provide symptomatic relief for severe anemia, it is a supportive measure that does not establish the underlying diagnosis causing pancytopenia.
(Choice C)
Viral serology testing
While viral infections like EBV, CMV, or parvovirus B19 can cause bone marrow suppression, establishing the diagnosis of aplastic anemia through bone marrow evaluation is the immediate priority before investigating potential triggers.
(Choice D)
Peripheral blood flow cytometry
Flow cytometry is useful for diagnosing hematologic malignancies or paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, but bone marrow evaluation takes priority to assess cellularity and exclude aplastic anemia.
(Choice E)
Bone marrow evaluation
Bone marrow biopsy and aspiration are required to confirm hypocellularity and diagnose aplastic anemia in the setting of pancytopenia with low reticulocyte response.

pages.question: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his colleague for an urgent behavioral assessment. The patient is a successful software engineer and a recent change in his demeanor caught the attention of his team lead. During the evaluation, he avoids maintaining eye contact and appears withdrawn during the conversation. When queried about his recent behavior, his colleague interjects, noting that the patient has seemed stressed and aloof, though still fulfilling his work responsibilities. The colleague remarks, "Perhaps medication to boost his morale would help." No reports of insomnia, altered appetite, or fatigue are noted. What would be the best step to further engage the patient in this setting?

answers.text:
Administer a mild anxiolytic and attempt the interview again.
(0%)

Inform the patient that an absence of dialogue may lead to hospitalization.
(0%)

Request the colleague to help the patient articulate his feelings.
(0%)

Initiate a comprehensive physical assessment immediately.
(0.71%)

Politely ask the colleague to step outside so you can speak with the patient privately.
(99.29%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Ensuring a private interaction between patient and clinician is crucial as it fosters an environment of trust, vital for patients who may hesitate to disclose personal details in the presence of others. This setting could reveal underlying issues such as anxiety, depression, or even domestic concerns that the patient may be reluctant to share publicly.
(Choice A)
Administer a mild anxiolytic and attempt the interview again.
Administering anxiolytics or sedatives without proper assessment and informed consent is inappropriate. Medication should not be used to facilitate communication when simple environmental modifications (privacy) would be more effective and ethical.
(Choice B)
Inform the patient that an absence of dialogue may lead to hospitalization.
Threatening hospitalization is coercive and can damage the therapeutic relationship. This approach violates patient autonomy and may cause the patient to become more withdrawn rather than encouraging open dialogue.
(Choice C)
Request the colleague to help the patient articulate his feelings.
Although the colleague seems well-intentioned, having a third party speak for the patient can inhibit honest communication and violates the principle of direct patient-provider interaction. Patients need privacy to openly discuss sensitive mental health concerns.
(Choice D)
Initiate a comprehensive physical assessment immediately.
While a physical exam can gradually build trust, speaking to the patient privately should be prioritized.
(Choice E)
Politely ask the colleague to step outside so you can speak with the patient privately.
The optimal action, as patients deserve an opportunity to discuss their issues in a confidential setting, free from outside influence, which can improve trust and communication.

pages.question: A 79-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, atrial fibrillation, and moderate dementia is transferred to a skilled nursing facility for post-acute rehabilitation following treatment for a hospital-acquired pneumonia. Her medications include apixaban, metformin, lisinopril, donepezil, and omeprazole. On admission, the Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA) screening tool identifies her as at risk for malnutrition. She has a stage III pressure injury on her right heel noted on transfer documentation. Her weight is 54 kg and height is 160 cm (BMI 21.1 kg/m²). Serum creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. The nursing staff notes she frequently refuses meals and appears to have reduced appetite. Which of the following best describes the most appropriate protein intake target and a key contributing factor to her poor appetite that should be addressed?

answers.text:
Target protein intake of 1.2 g/kg/day; poor appetite is due to omeprazole-induced hypergastrinemia and should be addressed by adding an H2-receptor antagonist
(0%)

Target protein intake of 1.0 g/kg/day; poor appetite is most likely caused by apixaban-induced gastrointestinal effects and should be addressed by switching to warfarin
(0%)

Target protein intake of 2.5 g/kg/day; poor appetite is due to metformin-induced vitamin B12 deficiency and requires intramuscular B12 injection
(0%)

Target protein intake of 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day for pressure injury healing; donepezil and omeprazole are common contributors to appetite suppression and nausea that should be reviewed
(33.33%)

Target protein intake of 0.6 g/kg/day to protect renal function; poor appetite is primarily due to dementia-related feeding difficulties and cannot be pharmacologically addressed
(66.67%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
For older adults with active pressure injuries in post-acute care, protein intake of 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day is recommended to support wound healing, even in the setting of mild-to-moderate CKD where the benefit of wound healing generally outweighs the risk of modest additional renal burden. Polypharmacy-related appetite suppression is highly prevalent in long-term care; agents such as donepezil and omeprazole commonly contribute to nausea, reduced appetite, and altered taste — all reversible if recognized and managed. Structured malnutrition screening tools like the MNA should trigger a formal dietitian assessment and individualized nutrition care plan.
(Choice A)
Target protein intake of 1.2 g/kg/day; poor appetite is due to omeprazole-induced hypergastrinemia and should be addressed by adding an H2-receptor antagonist
Although 1.2 g/kg/day is appropriate for general malnutrition prevention in older adults, it falls short of the 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day recommended for active pressure injury healing. While omeprazole does contribute to appetite suppression through micronutrient depletion and potential nausea, it does so primarily through zinc, magnesium, and B12 malabsorption — not hypergastrinemia. Adding an H2 blocker to a patient already on a proton pump inhibitor would be redundant and pharmacologically irrational, and would not address the nutritional consequences of prolonged acid suppression.
(Choice B)
Target protein intake of 1.0 g/kg/day; poor appetite is most likely caused by apixaban-induced gastrointestinal effects and should be addressed by switching to warfarin
While 1.0 g/kg/day meets the minimum RDA for older adults, it is insufficient for active pressure injury healing, which requires 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day. Apixaban is not a recognized cause of appetite suppression or nausea in clinical practice and switching to warfarin would not address nutritional concerns. Warfarin carries additional dietary restrictions (vitamin K consistency) that can further complicate nutritional management in older adults and is generally considered inferior to apixaban for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation.
(Choice C)
Target protein intake of 2.5 g/kg/day; poor appetite is due to metformin-induced vitamin B12 deficiency and requires intramuscular B12 injection
A protein target of 2.5 g/kg/day (135 g/day for this patient) exceeds evidence-based recommendations for pressure injury management (1.5-2.0 g/kg/day) and may impose unnecessary metabolic burden, particularly in a patient with CKD stage 3a. While metformin-associated vitamin B12 deficiency is well-documented and should be periodically assessed in long-term users, it typically develops gradually over years and manifests as neurological symptoms or megaloblastic anemia rather than acute appetite suppression. The patient's poor appetite is more likely related to her current medications (donepezil, omeprazole) that have immediate gastrointestinal effects. If B12 deficiency were confirmed, oral supplementation (1000-2000 mcg daily) is as effective as intramuscular injection for most patients with metformin-related deficiency.
(Choice D)
Target protein intake of 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day for pressure injury healing; donepezil and omeprazole are common contributors to appetite suppression and nausea that should be reviewed
National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel (NPIAP) and ESPEN guidelines recommend protein intake of 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day for patients with pressure injuries, as adequate protein is essential for collagen synthesis, immune function, and tissue regeneration. For this 54 kg patient, this translates to approximately 81–108 g of protein per day. CKD stage 3a does not warrant protein restriction sufficient to override the clinical priority of wound healing; nephrology consultation can guide individualized targets. Donepezil (a cholinesterase inhibitor) frequently causes gastrointestinal side effects including nausea, vomiting, and anorexia — administering it with food or switching to a patch formulation can reduce these effects. Omeprazole, through prolonged acid suppression, impairs absorption of zinc, magnesium, and vitamin B12, all of which play roles in wound healing and appetite regulation. A structured medication review targeting appetite-suppressing agents is a core component of nutritional rehabilitation in post-acute care. High-protein ONS between meals should be initiated alongside dietary counseling and a registered dietitian-led care plan.
(Choice E)
Target protein intake of 0.6 g/kg/day to protect renal function; poor appetite is primarily due to dementia-related feeding difficulties and cannot be pharmacologically addressed
Protein restriction to 0.6 g/kg/day is appropriate only in advanced CKD (typically stages 4–5) not on dialysis, and even then must be weighed against the risks of malnutrition. This patient has CKD stage 3a, where aggressive protein restriction is not routinely recommended and would significantly impair pressure injury healing. Furthermore, attributing poor appetite solely to dementia ignores the modifiable contribution of polypharmacy; donepezil commonly causes nausea and anorexia that can be mitigated by dose timing adjustments or formulation changes.

pages.question:

He reports 3-4 loose stools per day, occasionally awakening him from sleep, but no abdominal pain, weight loss, or blood in the stool. His medical history is notable for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed 18 months ago for symptomatic cholelithiasis. He has tried over-the-counter loperamide with minimal relief. Physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies are shown below. Colonoscopy with biopsies shows no evidence of inflammation or microscopic colitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?



Hemoglobin	13.4 g/dL
Hematocrit	41%
Red blood cell count	4.7 x10^6/µL
White blood cell count	7200/µL
Neutrophils	58%
Lymphocytes	32%
Monocytes	6%
Eosinophils	3%
Basophils	1%
Platelet count	260000/µL
Sodium	138 mEq/L
Potassium	4.1 mEq/L
Chloride	102 mEq/L
Bicarbonate	24 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen	14 mg/dL
Serum creatinine	0.9 mg/dL
Glucose	92 mg/dL
Calcium	9.4 mg/dL
Total protein	7.2 g/dL
Albumin	4.3 g/dL
Total bilirubin	0.8 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase	85 U/L
AST	22 U/L
ALT	20 U/L
Magnesium	1.9 mg/dL
Thyroid stimulating hormone	2.0 µIU/mL
Tissue transglutaminase IgA	Negative
Endomysial antibody	Negative
Stool culture	Negative
Stool ova and parasites	Negative
Clostridioides difficile toxin	Negative
Fecal calprotectin	Normal

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has bile acid diarrhea as a complication of prior cholecystectomy, presenting with chronic secretory diarrhea that persists during fasting. First-line therapy is a bile acid-binding resin such as cholestyramine.
(Choice A)
Budesonide
Budesonide is used for inflammatory conditions like microscopic colitis or Crohn's disease, but biopsies ruled out inflammation, so it is not indicated.
(Choice B)
Psyllium fiber supplement
Psyllium is a bulk-forming fiber supplement that can help with some types of diarrhea by absorbing water and forming gel-like stools. However, it does not address bile acid malabsorption and may actually worsen secretory diarrhea by increasing stool volume without treating the underlying cause.
(Choice C)
Probiotics
Probiotics may help restore gut microbiota balance and have some benefit in certain types of diarrhea, but they are not effective for bile acid malabsorption. The pathophysiology here involves excess bile acids irritating the colon, which requires specific bile acid sequestration rather than microbiota manipulation.
(Choice D)
Loperamide
Loperamide is an antimotility agent that slows intestinal transit and can provide symptomatic relief for diarrhea. However, the patient has already tried loperamide with minimal relief, and it does not address the underlying pathophysiology of bile acid malabsorption causing secretory diarrhea.
(Choice E)
Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine is a bile acid-binding resin that sequesters bile acids in the intestine, preventing their irritant effect on the colon and alleviating secretory diarrhea in bile acid malabsorption syndromes, such as post-cholecystectomy diarrhea.

pages.question: A 4-year-old Hispanic boy is brought to the clinic with complaints of arm pain and limited movement. According to the guardian, the boy suddenly began crying while playing on the playground when an older child swung him around by the arm. Upon examination, the boy holds his right arm close to his body in a semi-flexed position and resists attempts to extend or rotate the arm. No bruising, swelling, or obvious deformities are visible. A palpable 'click' is felt upon gentle supination of the forearm while flexing the elbow, immediately improving the child's comfort and range of motion. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The condition commonly known as nursemaid's elbow involves the displacement of the radial head from its normal anatomical position beneath the annular ligament. This occurs due to tensile force on an extended and pronated arm, often when a child's hand or wrist is pulled suddenly. The immediate relief observed upon reduction confirms the diagnosis, differentiating it from more severe injuries, such as fractures or ligament tears, which present with different clinical signs.
(Choice A)
Little Leaguer's elbow
